speechtext:
That this House condemns the Government's failure in bilateral relations with the United States with particular reference to:
1.	the failure to obtain an agreement from the United States to make a
commitment to early action on its share of environmental damage due to acid
rain; and
2.	the failure to make specific, that Canada would not participate in any
way in the star wars project of the United States.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Canadians and Americans across the border have been witnessing what the media have dubbed as the Shamrock Conference. Some have said that nothing was involved in the process which took place over a 24-hour period in Quebec City but a lot of media hype. Would that this were true. Regrettably it is not. Canadians and Americans have in fact seen what could perhaps be accurately described as the "Shamrock Shuffle", with President Reagan calling the tune and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) eagerly dancing along, taking us as a nation in an entirely new direction in terms of our relationship with the United States of America.
The resolution before the House, Mr. Speaker, refers to the failure of this Government's bilateral relationships with the United States, with particular reference to the continental problem of acid rain and the immense global problem of President Reagan's star wars project and our link with it. The resolution does deal concretely with these two important instances, but the point I want to make is that what is involved goes well beyond even those two important items in its seriousness.
Our history as a nation can be seen in one sense as one long struggle against assimilation. There has been throughout the time those of us in this Chamber have lived, as well as our ancestors, a tension between the conflicting poles of nationalism on the one hand and continentalism on the other.
It is a very interesting point of Canadian history that the Conservative Party, since Sir John A. Macdonald, on virtually every issue of substance during a time when it was the Government, has been on the nationalist side. Sir John A.
Macdonald gave to Canada a new national policy. Robert Borden fought the Liberals of the day on the issue of reciprocity for what he deemed to be the Canadian interest. Bennett in the 1930s produced for Canada the CBC and Air Canada, standing up for what he perceived to be Canadian national interests in a continent which was dominated by the economic power and thrust of the United States of America. John Diefenbaker fought the campaign of 1957 on the issue of Canadian economic nationalism. He talked about the importance of Canadian control in certain key sectors of the Canadian economy. I would add, in relation to what is taking place in Central America today, that it was John Diefenbaker who resisted the pressures from the United States in 1959 to cut off relations with the new Government of Cuba. It was John Diefenbaker, although there was some confusion on his policy in this regard because he was a Canadian nationalist and sensitive to the growing dangers of the proliferation of nuclear weapons, who, in the final analysis, refused to take nuclear weapons for the Bomarc missiles here in Canada.
Now there is a new kind of Conservativism. Since the election of September 4 we have witnessed what I would describe as a decisive shift in the history of the Conservative Party and, so far as they are able to get away with it, in the history of our country. The election of September 4 was the crowning point of the North American neo-conservative conti-nentalist movement that began in the 1970s and scored its first victory in 1980 with the election of President Reagan, and put the icing on the cake with the election of Brian Mulroney in Canada.

What has happened since the election? We have witnessed the impact of the Government's continentalism. First, they terminated FIRA. Then they made cutbacks in funding for the arts. What is the result for the economy? Since September, the Conservatives have simply approved all FIRA applications still pending.
Then came the summit. Two basic issues were on the agenda. First of all, acid rain and the damage it does to our buildings, the air we breathe, the water in our lakes, and our forests. Initially, President Reagan only had a report in mind-
But, Mr. Speaker, Brian got tough. In the earlier days of negotiations leading up to the summit meeting in Quebec City, he said through his officials: "Ronnie, a report is not good enough. The people of Canada are sensitive to the need for

definite action on acid rain. Therefore I can't, as Prime Minister, go back merely with a commitment to make a report". So he laid down the law. On behalf of the people of Canada he said that rather than having only a report we must do something decisive. We got something decisive: we got a further study.
Over 3,000 studies have been done on the problem of acid rain, but the decisive new leadership that we have in Canada now on the important problem of acid rain tells the Americans that we need 3,001 studies. He went even further. He said: "You appoint an envoy on your side, Ronnie, and we'll appoint one on ours. Of course, we will not give them any mandate to take effective action and we won't give them any budget. We will pay them a dollar a year and they will get a lot of media attention. A year from now they can come back and tell us how much worse the problem has gotten because nothing was done. Then we'll have a look at it again".
I would like to say to the Government of Canada that the people of Canada are fed up with this kind of action. Our buildings are literally decaying. Our beautiful lakes are dying. Our forests are being multilated and our health is threatened. In the face of this they propose another study with an envoy added who will make a report. What an envoy they have selected for Canada, "Mr. Decisiveness" himself, Bill Davis. I want to say something about-

speechtext:
There are a lot of indifferent and uncaring jerks who have been elected around the world. That is not our definition of success.
Let us consider Mr. Davis' record on acid rain. This is the man who is going to stand up in Washington for Canada's interests on acid rain. First consider Ontario Hydro, Mr. Speaker. It is the third largest producer of acid rain in North America. Four years ago Ontario Hydro had a level of emissions reaching 600,000 tonnes. The Ministry of the Environment ordered it to cut this deplorable level of emissions to 300,000 tonnes by 1990. How did this Ontario Crown corporation responsible to Bill Davis' Government respond? Hydro said that it would instal the scrubbers necessary to make this possible, but then decided not to. Consequently, Hydro's production of emissions actually increased last year by an additional 4,000 tonnes. There is a wonderful record of a Crown corporation under the responsibility of Bill Davis!
M5)
Let us consider Inco in the Province of Ontario. Inco happens to be the largest producer of acid rain in North America. In 1970, Inco was producing 5,200 tonnes of sulphur dioxide per day. This was increasing health damage to people
in this province and indeed in the United States. It was destroying our forests and polluting our lakes with those emissions day after day. What did the Ontario Government do under Bill Davis, that man of decisive action and commitment who is now going to speak to the United States Government on behalf of Canadians? The Government set out its standard in 1970 with the objective that the level of emissions should be reduced to 750 tonnes by 1978. In 1980, two years beyond the target set by the Government, it was producing three times the amount of the level of 2,500 tonnes set by the Conservatives. The Government had approved that level as a maximum, which was to be lowered to 1,950 tonnes by 1983.
The present performance of Inco seems to have made some progress if one considers it on an annual basis and compares it to recent years. However, if we consider the fact that there have been cut-backs in production as a result of massive lay-offs, the limited gains, that are nowhere near the standards set by the Government, virtually disappear.
I have said publicly that there are a number of things that Mr. Davis, as Premier, has done that have been good for the Province of Ontario. However, I suggest to the Hon. Member opposite who raised questions that Mr. Davis is the last person in the world to be fighting on our behalf about problems with acid rain, in this province or anywhere else.
I regret that the Prime Minister, who has talked about the importance of Parliament, could not be here on such a decisively important occasion following the summit. He spent a wonderful 48 hours parading in Quebec City. This debate flows directly from that summit and will involve the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) and the Liberals as well as our Party. He ought to have been here for this important occasion.
Rather than set up another study calling for another report on acid rain, with an envoy whose credentials are not the best, to put it euphemistically, the Prime Minister ought to have told President Reagan that since Canada is prepared to put up a certain amount of money for this study, the Americans should contribute the same proportionate amount.
While I praise the Government for its decision to deal with acid rain, I am talking about bilateral relations. As I said the other day, the Prime Minister has decided to be a kid brother to Ronald Reagan instead of a good neighbour. He should have told the President of the United States that since his country has produced half of the acid rain problem that exists in Canada, the very least it should do as a nation is put up proportionately what Canada has put up to address this problem. In other words, he should have said that the United States ought to have put up somewhere between $1 billion and $1.5 billion to show the people of Canada that they want to be a good neighbour to Canadians. Such a message by the Prime Minister would have been a demonstration of some kind of Canadian leadership-not to demand more of the Americans but to demand proportionately what we are prepared to do ourselves.
March 19, 1985

I do not think the ink had dried on the negotiating papers leading up to the statement that was to be made on acid rain before we had an official from the State Department already saying to American journalists: "Don't be taken in, fellas; President Reagan has not changed his position on acid rain at all". There has been no departure in terms of policy for the Americans on acid rain, no change; it was all one massive PR exercise.
It seems to me the Canadian Government realized who it was dealing with when it comes to acid rain. Mr. Reagan has all the sensitivity in terms of the environment that you could expect of a man who said not many years ago when he was a politician in California and the problems of the forests in California were brought to his attention: "When you have seen one tree, you have seen them all". There is a man who is sensitive to the needs of the environment; his name, Ronald Reagan.
I am saying that our approach is not good enough. We should have demanded proportional action, and if we did not get it our Prime Minister could have come back with dignity. He could have said: "I went to bargain with the Americans. I did my best. We have our act together on acid rain here. We asked them to do proportionately what we did, but they said no". " I regret" he could have told us, "that we have decided to agree to disagree. I promised the people of Canada that I will continue with the struggle to get the Americans to pay their way, to do their share and to stop putting their garbage on our side of the fence". He could have come back with dignity even if he had lost the particular battle, as we do from time to time with our strong neighbour to the south, and he would have maintained the respect of all Canadians who are concerned about acid rain. Instead, he attempted to do a great smokescreen exercise, a PR exercise, that is worse than useless because it leaves the impression that something might be done with acid rain when it will not deal with the issue one bit.

There he is, the master of facts, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark). We will hear his brave contribution in a minute. A couple of years ago this scheme was proposed by President Reagan. Almost the whole world knows about it now. It is a plan to destroy ICBMs and intermediate range missiles before they reach the target. That is the scheme. It is also a scheme that is likely to involve the
Supply
spending of some $70 to $100 billion between now and 1993 in the United States, according to the priorities set out by President Reagan.
The important point about this scheme is that it came from Mr. Reagan and a handful of his advisers. It was attacked by the Republicans in Congress. It was attacked by the Democrats in Congress. It was attacked by defence experts. It was attacked by church groups. It has, in fact, been attacked by western allies of the United States, who have temporarily kept quiet, as being either totally irrational as a concept for defence on the one hand, or destabilizing on the other, or both.
John Lamb, Executive Director of the Canadian Centre for Arms Control and Disarmament, when he was echoing a widespread sentiment by defence experts on both sides of the Atlantic Ocean, said this about it:
It is clear that star wars would severely upset the balance of East-West deterrence.
Even our late and unlamented former Minister of National Defence said last fall in one of the early give-aways that it would "fundamentally change the strategic relationship". If that does not mean it would be destabilizing in terms of East-West discussions in detente, I do not know what else it could mean.
The recent debate in Canada has focused on the link between star wars and our own defence policy, particularly with the updating of the DEW line of the North Warning System.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the consideration of all Hon. Members of the House. Of course, we will reciprocate in terms of the other principal speakers.
When it comes to discussions of the star wars project and its linkage, or potential linkage, with the updating of our own DEW line, U.S. officials have repeatedly said that there was a linkage. On the other hand, Canadian Cabinet Ministers have repeatedly said the opposite. I would just like to put some of these comments on the record.
On January 16, Secretary of Defense Weinberger said that star wars, if deployed, would have to be backed up by an updated DEW line. He saw a linkage. The former Minister of National Defence, the Hon. Member for Cumberland-Col-chester (Mr. Coates), said just about a week later that there was no connection between star wars and the DEW line. Act three-Paul Nitze, key adviser on defence matters in the United States and a distinguished gentleman, said on March 6 that he acknowledged there could be a connection between star wars and the DEW line in the future. Our own Secretary of State for External Affairs, who always has his facts right, then

March 19, 1985
Supply
said: "There is absolutely no connection between star wars and the DEW line". Richard Burt, a man who advises Canadian journalists, in doing what is called a backgrounder on the visit of President Reagan to our country, said: "Oh yes, there is a connection between star wars and the DEW line". Then when a reporter said: "Oh my goodness, the Canadian Government said the opposite", Mr. Burt said: "Oh my goodness, I made a mistake". Of course, the mistake was not what he had said in terms of its actual accuracy; his mistake was an error in judgment-he told the truth and he was not supposed to be telling us what it was all about.
As the Prime Minister always likes to do, I will leave the last word on this matter to President Reagan. Just yesterday President Reagan made an incredible speech, in many ways, on the eve of his departure from Canada. He included the following:
We look forward to the possibility of sharing new developments in SD1 technology with Canada.
He certainly sees some kind of possible or potential link arising from the openness of the Government of Canada, not the people of Canada, toward this project.

I wish he would get hold of the article released yesterday by Mr. Genscher, the Foreign Secretary of West Germany, who has raised many questions about star wars. If that does not cause him to think a little more, maybe he would look at the one by Geoffrey Howe, the British Foreign Secretary, who is certainly saying one thing privately to other members of NATO which expresses his serious concern about the star wars initiative and indeed is saying things publicly which express a great deal of concern about the project. We would like to see this coming from the Government of Canada, not simply from Great Britain and West Germany.
The points are very clear. Star wars is a destabilizing concept and initiative. It was opposed not only by Canadians; it was opposed, to his credit, by Walter Mondale in the United States. It has been opposed by many defence officials in the United States. It has been opposed by men and women around the world who want the Soviet Union and the United States to start de-escalating the armaments race instead of getting it going on an even higher track. The Government of Canada either has to be naive about this or misleading, or both, and the people of Canada can make their judgment. In either case, the people of Canada do not want any connection with the star wars project.
I want now to conclude my observations. I say as a person who has spent some time studying Canadian history and has just made a very brief reference to virtually every Conservative Prime Minister since Confederation, that there is a new drift. There is a clear departure from the past Conservative traditions. I say that this continentalist drift that is under way must be stopped.
Canadians do want to be good neighbours. We do want to be good friends. However, we recognize seriously that while our destinies are indeed connected, we must continue the struggle of our ancestors in this nation to build on our part of the continent a nation clearly linked by history and geography with our American friends and neighbours, but a nation clearly in command of its own political, military, economic and cultural decisions. Previous Conservative Governments in our history have understood that, in the final analysis, maintaining good relationships between neighbouring nations of unequal power requires constant vigilance on the part of Canada. It requires independence of thought, action and program. The new Conservative Government either does not understand this or, more alarmingly, does not care. The new Conservative Government has embarked upon the most radical change in Canada-U.S. relations in this century.
Misunderstanding the nature of loyalty, it is forgetting, as Escott Reid pointed out in a moving article in today's Citizen, that the loyal ally must at times oppose with all its determination the particular policies of its neighbour. Misunderstanding our own real cultural, economic and defence needs, the Conservative Government is prepared to leave us adrift on the tumultuous North American seas in the naive hope we can survive without a chart. Misunderstanding its obligation to provide confident leadership to Canadians, the new Government has decided to follow an American President. I urge strong support for the motion before the House.

One is left wondering if there was not in all the events of last weekend somewhat less than might have met the eye. From the attitude of the Government, the second line of that song would have been especially appropriate, and I wish the Prime Minister would have broken off into one of the well-known solos of his. That second line is "And nothing's plenty for me". You got it, Mr. Speaker!
In a more serious sense, with the greatest respect, we have witnessed in the past two days another example by this Government and this Prime Minister of what I call cosmetic politics where appearance takes precedence over reality, style

over substance and package over policy. It is an approach to government that seems directed more by desire to placate, a need to please, an urge to be loved, than the ability to order priorities and a willingness to make choices.
There is no doubt that in an increasingly dependent world, Canada and the United States enjoy a special, unique relationship. Many would say that that relationship is not only unique, but historically very special, and I agree. Our two countries share similar values, many interests and, while geography has made us neighbours, as the late President John Kennedy used to say, history has made us friends. We do not, however, share every interest. There are differences and they too are real and important. Underlining those differences should not be interpreted as traces of anti-Americanism, but as a real regard on behalf of the people of Canada to exercise our own priorities and our own preferences.
With respect to what President Reagan wanted for last weekend's meeting, what did he want? Clearly he wanted a continuation of what he had already got from this Government over the last six months-the abolition of FIRA, the dismantling of the National Energy Program, a renewal of our Radar Distant Warning System in the North, whether it is part of star wars or not only history will judge-

We have an amendment where we have taken our judgment because we believe what has happened, but you have not shown us-more Canadian troops for NATO; more study but no action on acid rain; and an example in Canada that the so-called nuclearology, and I am using American words, does not extend from New Zealand to North America.
We know what the President wanted because he told us. We know what he obtained. He obtained some of those things he perhaps deserved, and I do not criticize all of them in all of their aspects. But the question before this House is, what did we get? What did Canada get? For that matter, what did we want? We were not told what it was we wanted. We never saw the agenda. We in the House were never given a statement regarding Canada's priorities. Perhaps we should have wanted real and tangible progress on trade relations, but clearly the Government has not got its own act together regarding how far it wishes to go with the United States on free trade. Our country was not in a position to push this matter.
We on this side of the House, members of this Party, are in favour of enhancing and advancing our goal of better neighbourhood. We are in favour of improving our trade relationships and exploring new relationships with the United States in a way that does not yield or sacrifice our Canadian manufacturing base or employment base. Those things are vital for jobs.
If we had a choice of neighbours, looking around the world, who would we rather have as a neighbour? Would we rather

be situated beside the Soviet Union or Mainland China? We are situated beside the most friendly group of people on the face of the earth and a great neighbour, I concede that. The point is that that relationship is an overwhelming one. Every Prime Minister of the country has had an opportunity to describe it. Yes, let us go for more trade but not at the expense of the independence of our foreign policy, the independence of our defence policy, our political sovereignty, our economic integrity or our cultural integrity. That is what worries us.

We feel that those principles might well have been breached over the weekend in Quebec City. Who was the big winner? I suppose I would put St. Patrick, the patron saint of Ireland, first. He was the undoubted winner.
The Prime Minister loves to weave tales about his modest upbringing as the barefoot boy from Baie Comeau. He likes to recall to his official biographer how he once sang for the then publisher of the Chicago Tribune who came to Baie Comeau to inspect his fiefdom, the Quebec North Shore Paper Company. The Prime Minister, as young Brian, used to sing American-Irish ditties for the colonel for which he would receive the odd $20. Well, the Prime Minister was singing for his supper again over the weekend. He is still singing.
The Prime Minister had his cap in hand. As a matter of fact, "Cap" got out of hand, did he not? The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Nielsen) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs had a lot of trouble with "Cap" until they finally got his CTV interview straightened out.
In any event, there was such a great atmosphere at the meeting. It is too bad it had to be interrupted by a bit of work. Not much work was done but some business got taken care of. There were advance press releases just to loosen up the party so they could have a good time. I am sorry the good time had to be interrupted by two hours' work.
The Prime Minister did a lot of preparatory work in order to get a deal on acid rain. He began by saying the kinds of things the U.S. administration loves to hear. He seems to think that the United States Government could make a case for taking no action. He told U.S. officials that our record on acid rain was not as good as theirs. He said we had to go to the table with clean hands. We on this side of the House have dealt with this matter before. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), has dealt with it very explicitly.
The Prime Minister threw our cards away before he ever got to the bargaining table. Never mind that we had a program to reduce sulphur dioxide emissions by 25 per cent by 1990 and 50 per cent by 1994 and the U.S. had no such program. Never mind that the United States produces 19.6 million tonnes of nitrous oxide per year while we produce only 1.7 million tonnes. The Prime Minister gave the President of the United States an easy way out. He threw away our bargaining chips before he ever got to the table.
After laying that solid groundwork, the Prime Minister did try to recover. In preparation for the Summit meeting, the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Blais-Grenier) announced a plan to spend $300 million over the next 10 years to combat acid rain. The Hon. Member for Oshawa has been very explicit with respect to acid rain. Real progress in this area is measured by the definition of standards as goals. It is measured by agreement on regulations to promote those goals and the expenditure of money to meet those standards. We did not get any of that. Instead, we got special envoys and we will have more study and more talk.

Mr. Speaker, let me begin, if I might, by saying to the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner), as someone who has suffered through that position and knows all of its delights and limitations, that I thought he delivered today a very amusing and careful speech. At the beginning of my political career I remember very well what happened with the Bomarc. There was an agreement. It was signed in good will with the Americans, and so on. When Mr. Diefenbaker realized that there was to be a deployment of the Bomarc in Canada, he said that it was not what he had intended and he backed away. At that time we said that if we had signed the agreement we had to respect our word. I remember I had a problem about voting on it myself. I talked with Mr. Harkness, a great gentleman, and asked him whether we were committed. He said: "Mr. Chretien, a Tory I am". There was no greater Conservative in spirit or at heart than he. He said that Canada had given its word and that he had to accept it. That was why he resigned from Cabinet. When that agreement was signed in 1957, no one knew exactly what would be the consequences. However, it took Canada 22 years to get out of it. It was only last summer that the last Bomarc left Canada. Now we have no nuclear warheads on our soil.
What are we doing now? In the north we are letting them build large airstrips. Mr. Weinberger said over the weekend that the missiles, the defense weapons, would be located where it was best. In Canada we have been unanimous in the House; even today the Government told us that it was opposed to the deployment of any nuclear arms on Canadian soil. When it makes such a statement, it has to take the step to ensure that it never happens. This is why we are critical of the Government, because of its ambivalence in that regard. It is because we believe it is a new escalation. The Russians will not let the Americans do it and not match it. When we were in government we had to make some very difficult decisions. We permitted testing of the Cruise missile in Canada. We were in favour of the two-track policy. We had an impression, or even a conviction, that the U.S.S.R. had gone ahead, so we decided to conduct more tests in an attempt to arrive at an equilibrium between the quality of armaments on both sides.
What is the other side of the two-track policy? After we have virtually reached that plateau, suffocation is supposed to come, reduction is supposed to come. SDI is against this idea. It is a new step forward. It has always been like that since 1941. It has always been a research program. When the Manhattan project was developed during the war, it was a research program.
At this time I am reading a book on Truman. Days before he dropped the bomb on Hiroshima, there was a debate in the U.S. administration as to whether it should explode the bomb in the Bay of Tokyo and not hurt any people. It would have

I do not know what they are up to with SDL I am not a scientist. There is much controversy about it around the world at this time, not only in Canada. The external affairs minister for England talked about that. Everyone talks about it. There has been a lot of pressure. Everyone comes onside eventually, but everyone has a lot of apprehension about it. We have apprehension. What worries me is what happens after a mistake is made.
Again in Quebec City yesterday, Defence Secretary Weinberger said: "Of course, it might be in Canada". We could have attributed that to an error, to a slip of the tongue a few months ago, but he said it again yesterday. Two weeks ago a press reporter asked Paul Nitze about it and he said "Of course". After that they clarified it. It is an indication that in the minds of the Americans they have no doubt. Of course, they say they will respect the jurisdiction of Canada. Of course, Margaret Thatcher could have said no to deployment. Of course, the Germans could have said no to deployment eventually. Some are still trying. However, when we create the climate or the environment, we are trapped and the pressure is on us.
That is exactly why we are asking the question. If it is for the good of Canada and if it is rationally explained to us, we might say yes; but as a Canadian I believe we are making a fundamental mistake in playing our cards like that. It is one thing to say to the Americans that they are welcome in Canada, that Canada is for sale and so on, but look what happened with the flow of capital in September. It has not flowed south-north, it has flowed north-south.
Look at the market. In one week there was such an outflow of capital from Canada, for many reasons, that the Government had to borrow $2.5 billion. Why? It was because American money was leaving Canada and we had to buy Canadian dollars. We had no choice. That is the reality.
As my Leader said a few minutes ago, the Americans are our best friends. What do we expect from our best friends? We expect respect and truth. I do not need anybody to pat my back. I hope my friends will come to me and tell me the truth. Those are real friends.
Very often we can be useful to the Americans, if we are not seen as the fifty-first state. We can be useful because we are a different country. We have access to some countries to which they do not.
I remember the last day I was Minister of Finance in 1979. I signed an agreement with Algeria. I asked why they wanted to do business with Canada. They told me it was because Canada is the only country in the world which could give them North American technology in French. Some 40 countries around the world have French as their first or second language. They look to Canada. Any Member of this House who travels abroad knows that they do not receive the same reaction when they show their Canadian passport. That is because we have a credibility of our own. The Americans are different. Some people look at them as having imperialist ideas. I do not look at them in that way. I do not say that they have. However, some people do believe that.
Canadians do not have any ambition like that. Canadians can go anywhere in the world with a different approach. Sometimes that can be very useful. We have not done everything that has been accomplished since 1867 to end up in 1985 wondering whether one day we will still be a country. You cannot rest all your faith for the future on Washington. speechtext:
Interests do differ. Governing the United States is not an easy task. I have had dealings with American Governments for 17 years and I witnessed the frustration of their administration. Administering Canada may be difficult,
March 19, 1985

but nowhere near as much as administering the United States. More often than not protective measures are taken by American States, and when that happens there is practically nothing the central American Government can do about it. That is the kind of experience we have every day. For instance, the enforcement of American extraterritorial legislation which we are regularly faced with and about which the administration does not do anything.
Another recent problem which I want to raise in the House today-good relations are fine, but Canadian interests ought to come first-concerns a Canadian bank that was forced to break another country's law to meet the requirements of the American administration.

A few months ago there was a situation in the United States where the Bank of Nova Scotia was forced to break the laws of a third country in order to avoid United States personnel being put in jail. What kind of friendship is that? What about our own integrity?
We had the same problems in the uranium cartel. The Americans were asking the Canadian company to do certain things. Foreign companies with the head office in the United States and a branch in Canada could do things which the law of Canada did not permit them to do. There are a lot of these situations. When you go there and say "I am a nice guy, I will sing along with you", you must remember that the Americans are tough bargainers. They are not kids. They have seen people before and they know the difference between a smile and strength. They always respect strength.
It is easy to have parties and it is sometimes easier to make people laugh, but when you talk about a country like Canada which has had great success with the Americans, you have to be sure that they know that we are neighbours and not assimilated within the system. It is very frustrating when you talk to those who take Canada for granted all the time. They do not like us to ask any questions. They are offended if we do ask questions.
There is not one week when I do not pick up a magazine which shows politicians blaming the administration for this and for that. There is not one day of the week when there is not a split in the White House on policy. Therefore, should we as Canadians not be able to say what we think? What kind of maturity is that? I am sure that the President of the United States would rather have a good, frank, open discussion on an issue than to have a pat on the back. I am sure that he would listen to a good argument. Do not kid yourselves, the Americans love Canada, but they will invest in Canada only if they can make a buck. If they are going to lose money, they will not come here.
What we are very disappointed about is the lack of candour and the naivety of the Government. If the Government wants to make a deal with the Americans on SDI and wants to make Canada available for nuclear armaments, other countries have done it. Germany, England, Italy and other European countries have done it. There is no shame to it. However, do not try
to have it both ways. If you do not want it, say so. Do not create a situation where they will have the absolute right eventually to say it was not written down, but we created the condition whereby they could come if they wanted.
If you do not want to have somebody at your home on a Saturday night because you want a quiet evening, do not invite a bunch of your friends to come for a beer! Do not invite them if you do not want them. I have had that experience a few times.
It is a serious problem. The people of Canada want candour. They want the truth. If we act as a senior partner with the Americans and we treat them as an equal, even if we are smaller in terms of population, they will respect us. However, if we just play to their cue, if we just go and sing for them, they will be nice to us, but eventually we will lose our independence. Canadians from sea to sea have put too much into building a society that is different, one that is our own, that we shall never be assimilated into the United States. We are too proud to be Canadian.

SEIZURE OF TURKISH EMBASSY-TRIBUTE TO OTTAWA POLICE FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, many of us celebrated the Feast of St. Patrick on Sunday, and some celebrated in splendid colour in Quebec city. As we refreshed our Irish heritage, we acknowledged the credit that St. Patrick deserves for his saintly efforts to bring the peaceful word to
Ireland. His risks were high and sometimes violent, but he did his job and met his challenge.
Last week in Ottawa an unacceptable terrorist attack took place at the Turkish Embassy that resulted in the tragic loss of life of a Pinkerton's security man, Mr. Claude Brunelle, and caused serious injuries to the Turkish ambassador, Ambassador Kirca. The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) spoke of the co-operative actions between the RCMP and the Ottawa Police Force. That is true, but I would like to underline the fact that the Ottawa Police took most of the risks in response to this unpredictable act of violence.
Protection of embassies in Ottawa is a federal responsibility, but any criminal offence that takes place within city property, whether it be public or private, federal or international in nature, in the Province of Ontario has traditionally become the immediate responsibility of the local police force. Within three minutes of being called, the Ottawa Police were on the scene. Constable Michel Prudhomme saw Ambassador Kirca lying on the ground and risked his own life by jumping a fence to pull the ambassador to safety.
A four-hour standoff ensued, under the command of Staff Inspector Wilfred Longchamps of the Ottawa Police. The terrorists were then arrested by his SWAT team, with no further loss of life. I am proud of the quick, efficient, brave and professional actions of the City of Ottawa Police. They did their job and also met their challenge. Let us give credit where credit is due.

EFFECT OF BUDGETARY CUT-BACKS ON REGIONAL PROGRAMMING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the cut-backs in CBC funding represent not only broken promises but disrupted services and lost opportunities. Regional programming has been especially badly hit, some regions more so than others. Newfoundland and Labrador have suffered some of the worst blows with the closing of the Gander station and the reduction of half of the sation in Labrador City.
The cuts in Gander have since been rescinded, showing that the CBC is able to respond with good sense to public outcry. It is time now for the cuts in Labrador City to be rescinded. Because of those cuts there will be no local TV programming whatsoever for a substantial area with no commercial stations.
Isolated parts of Canada vitally depend on the CBC. These are not the areas which should be cut. We have a national public broadcasting system. Its duty is to serve the whole of the country, including small and distant communities. It is a fact of life in Canada that services to such areas are costly for the size of the population served, but that is our country. Patriotic duty requires us all, urban and rural, south and north, to support necessary services for all parts of Canada.
It is time for this Parliament to send a message to Monsieur Juneau and the CBC to restore regional programming, rescind the cut-backs in Labrador City, and get on with the job of uniting Canadians.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON SECURITY AT TURKISH EMBASSY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when on March 15 I rose on a point of order. I indicated that I would initiate an investigation into possible approaches to the Government made since February 13 by officials of the Turkish Embassy in Ottawa regarding the security of their embassy. This investigation has established that the Government was indeed approached more recently than mid-February. Nevertheless, the investigation has also established that the RCMP acted immediately to increase their vigilance. In short, although Ministers were not

March 19, 1985
Turkish Embassy Security
directly involved with these contacts, the RCMP were, and the RCMP took action immediately.
There were two further contacts between Turkish and Canadian officials after mid-February. On February 22 there was a conversation between a representative of the Turkish Embassy and the Office of Protocol of my Department. That conservation dealt primarily with a separate issue concerning international terrorism, but the Turkish representative took the occasion to reiterate concern about the threat perceived to security of the embassy. That conversation was reported directly to the RCMP.
The second conversation occurred on March 5, when the RCMP visited the Turkish Embassy at their own initiative to discuss with embassy staff internal security provisions. At that meeting a representative of the Turkish Embassy discussed with the RCMP the level of threat to the embassy.
Before I made the statement in the House on March 14, I asked for detailed information on all contacts between Turkish officials and our Department. I was not told of the conversations that had taken place on February 22 and on March 5. As soon as I learned of them on March 15, I came back to the House to make my statement on a point of order.
Neither conversation conveyed a warning of a specific attack and neither provided new information going beyond what the Turkish authorities had given us in mid-February.
As I said last Friday, I respect this House and, once again, I apologize for inadvertently having conveyed incomplete information to the House. But I can assure the House that the missing information did not materially affect the assessment of threat to the security of the Turkish mission, and that in both cases the communications from the Turks were taken fully into account.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON SECURITY AT TURKISH EMBASSY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin my brief reply by thanking the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) for making a copy of his statement available to me during Question Period.
What emerges from a reading of this document is a picture of worried Turkish diplomats in this capital trying in one way and another to obtain increased security, seeking to meet with members of the RCMP to convey their concerns and seeking to meet with the Office of Protocol of the Minister's Department, again trying to receive increased security. If I can quote from a Minister in the Turkish Assembly again giving special warning to Canada, he asked that specific threats be responded to by increased levels of security.
The Minister has not succeeded in bailing out the Government on this one by the statement he has made. A few days ago in the House, on March 13, the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) indicated, as reported on page 2969 of Hansard, that increased security was provided at the Turkish Embassy. What the Secretary of State for External Affairs has said today is slightly different from what was in the written statement I received. What he said was that the RCMP took action immediately in the sense of increasing security, as the Deputy Prime Minister has said.
This allegation by the Government that increased security is contradicted by the facts. It is contradicted by people of Pinkerton's who indicated that no change at all occurred as a result of the review of security which took place 30 days before the incident.
I think the Government owes it to the House to come clean with us and, if it claims that the RCMP took action and that increased security was provided, it should indicate what was done. Their assertions and their attempts to bail themselves out are contradicted by others who I think ought to be believed. I want to ask whether the House is being misled by the statements which have been made on this occasion, in addition to what increased security was provided to these worried Turkish diplomats who were attempting to obtain it.
The RCMP provided a report to the Government which I commissioned but did not receive. It was given to the new Government. That report for increased security sat with the Government for six months without being taken to Cabinet, according to the Solicitor General (Mr. MacKay).
I also feel entitled to ask whether there were measures recommended by the RCMP which were not put into effect by the Government, which were not responded to positively by the Government.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON SECURITY AT TURKISH EMBASSY

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON SECURITY AT TURKISH EMBASSY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in his statement the Minister apologizes "for inadvertently having conveyed incomplete information to the House". The Minister did not convey incomplete information. What was told to the House was wrong; it was not a matter of being incomplete. The Minister and the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) categorically denied that there had been, subsequent to the meetings which they affirmed did take place between Government representatives and the Turkish Embassy, any other meetings of any kind to discuss security at the Turkish Embassy. Therefore, it was not a matter of incomplete information, I say to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark); it was a question of wrong information.
Frankly, I am angry at the tone of the statement, that the Minister would suggest that some kind of appropriate action
March 19, 1985

was taken after the Turkish Embassy made it known (a) to Ministry officials and (b) to the RCMP that they had reason to believe that there was an increased threat to their embassy. For the Minister to suggest that some kind of appropriate action was taken is again wrong. There was no action taken of any substance.
There was one guard at the embassy in advance and there was one guard after the information was conveyed to the Minister or the Ministry and the RCMP. That guard was not adequately trained. That guard was not given additional backup. That guard was not provided with additional support in order that he could do the job that he was being inadequately paid to do.
It is with a sense of frustration that I listened to and read the Minister's statement. I would have accepted it if the Secretary of State for External Affairs had simply said that he had been given wrong information, that he apologized and that the information that he had subsequently been given was in fact consistent with what Opposition Members had been suggesting took place. However, to try to colour it in such a way as to make it appear that there was some kind of deliberate action taken either by the RCMP or by the Ministry in response to a plea for help from the Turkish Embassy is to deny the truth in the instance.
I also want to say to the Minister that given the level of protection that was afforded, given that there was a clear state of high alert as a result of the Orly airport trials and the pending trials here, given that that had been conveyed around the world by the Turkish Government, given that that had been on the agenda of the world security services of Interpol and therefore on the agenda of our security service, what was done was wrong and what is being said in the statement is unacceptable.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON SECURITY AT TURKISH EMBASSY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to pose a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark). I am told on fairly good authority that after the demonstrations which occur on, I think, April 24, an Armenian day of celebration, there is frequently a high alert and demonstrations. I understand that either last year or the year before after such a demonstration, the Turkish ambassador came to the then Secretary of State for External Affairs with the actual rock that had gone through the window of his embassy and landed on his writing desk. He took it to the previous Liberal Government and indicated "I need more protection, especially around this period of April 24". I want to know if the Secretary of State for External Affairs can confirm that, whether he has seen that in his report. Can he indicate what the Ministry will do in the future around April 24 at the time of those kinds of demonstrations to protect the Turkish Embassy, so that those kinds of things will not happen again?

Mr. Speaker, I think you will agree that it would be inappropriate for me to comment on matters that might have happened regarding former Ministers and former administrations. I can say that I know nothing of that situation. I cannot report more fully on it.
Turkish Embassy Security
With regard to the situation of the Turkish Embassy here and elsewhere, the House knows of the extreme sensitivity of that question. We have taken actions at the Turkish Embassy which in the middle of February last year the Turkish Embassy deemed to be satisfactory. Naturally we are going to look at the matter again. The Hon. Member would not want me or anyone else in this House to discuss details of security arrangements in ways that might increase the danger for individual embassies or individual representatives of other countries in Canada or elsewhere.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON SECURITY AT TURKISH EMBASSY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question relates to the suggestion that the Canadian Security Intelligence Service, pursuant to its mandate to deal with terrorism and suspected terrorism in Canada, may not have alerted the RCMP, responsible for the enforcement of the law, to the heightened sense of danger which was posed in the circumstances surrounding this particular incident. I want to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) specifically whether CSIS did inform the RCMP and of the fact that they viewed this as a very serious matter. If CSIS did inform the RCMP of that, what specific steps did the RCMP take to respond to that heightened degree of concern on the part of CSIS?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON SECURITY AT TURKISH EMBASSY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, for reasons the House will understand, I do not propose to discuss publicly specific steps that have been taken or might be taken, because that kind of discussion could very seriously jeopardize the security of the people we are trying to protect. Indeed, it could have the consequence, which no one here would intend or want, of putting them into greater danger. I indicated in my statement, and I repeat it now, that when information came to the attention of the Government, while to my great regret Ministers were not informed, the RCMP was informed and acted.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON SECURITY AT TURKISH EMBASSY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want at this time to repeat briefly questions that I asked during my statement because they have not, understandably, been addressed yet by the Minister. When the Minister says that the RCMP took action immediately, does he mean by that that the level of security at the Turkish Embassy was increased?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON SECURITY AT TURKISH EMBASSY

I am sure that the former Solicitor General, as a former Minister of the Crown responsible for security activities, would not want me to get into detail on the floor of the House of Commons as to exactly what action was taken. He should know better than others that action that might have been taken in the case of an urgent situation there might also be taken in others. To reply to that kind of question would indicate patterns of response by the Government of Canada that would have the effect of putting in danger the very people we are trying to protect.

Mr. Speaker, whatever pattern of security was put into place, it is obvious that it failed and failed miserably, to have one Pinkerton guard guarding the embassy. I would like the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) to explain what appears to be a very obvious inconsistency. The RCMP inspector in charge of VIP protection in Ottawa stated that there was no stepped-up security prior to the incident because there was no intelligence information indicating that it might be needed. That is from the The Globe and Mail of March 13, 1985. Here we have the Secretary of State for External Affairs saying that there was stepped-up security. We have the RCMP inspector saying that there was no stepped-up security because there was no intelligence available.
Can the Secretary of State for External Affairs clarify the obvious inconsistency? Could he also indicate whether the RCMP, when it was given this advance warning, advised the Solicitor General (Mr. MacKay) of the advance warning and whether the Security Intelligence Service was involved and was advised of this advance warning?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have one final question to put to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark). The RCMP were aware of the Turkish Embassy's concerns, and as 1 understand it, there was also additional information available to them with regard to the level of threat which was in existence not only in Canada but in other parts of the world at the time the Turkish Embassy brought to the attention of the RCMP its concerns about its own security. Does the Secretary of State believe that the actions taken by the RCMP in response to those threats, given the professional nature of that force and the responsibility it has not only to enforce law and order but to protect diplomats in Canada, were adequate?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON SECURITY AT TURKISH EMBASSY

Mr. Speaker, as I have said before and as the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) has said, no one would pretend that response was adequate when security arrangements were breached. We all know that. We deeply regret that.
I suppose that the response that is in question, the response that troubles me, has to do with the response of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) and the response of the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent), who were genuinely invited by the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) to co-operate with us in this most sensitive matter, a matter which has traditionally been the subject of co-operation between Governments and Opposition Parties. They refused to take part in that kind of common action to try to deal with a major security problem. Instead of helping us solve the problem, the Opposition Parties have been trying to find ways to raise questions in the House of Commons which would not help the diplomats but which could have the effect of helping the terrorists.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in support of the motion moved by the Hon. Member for Oshawa and seconded by the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) which is critical of the Government for a number of reasons pertaining to the recent summit meeting between the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and President Reagan. I would like to concentrate on that aspect of the motion which has to do with acid rain.
I would like to begin by saying that I implied in Question Period, Mr. Speaker, that is, by coming out of the summit meeting in the way the Prime Minister did with an agreement to the appointment of high level envoys from each country who would be responsible for a mutual study of the problem of acid rain, the Prime Minister in effect conceded to the American view of the acid rain problem. It is as simple as that, Mr. Speaker. The American view, well known and not hidden, is that more research needs to be done on acid rain and that no action should be taken until there is more conclusive evidence that acid rain is actually as harmful as many people say it is. That is the American position. Perhaps I should say that that is the position of the present American administration and of President Reagan because, clearly, there are different views of the acid rain problem within the United States itself and it is somewhat inaccurate to talk continually about the American position as if it was totally homogeneous.
The position as expressed by President Reagan has been that more research is needed and that action at this time is not



March 19, 1985
Supply
appropriate. The position of the Canadian Government, to its credit, is to act to reduce acid rain. I say "to its credit" because it has become a kind of knee-jerk response on the part of the Government to accuse us of always being negative. I was not negative some weeks ago when the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Blais-Grenier) made the announcement with respect to the action the Government was going to take with respect to acid rain. I hope people will keep that in mind and that my criticisms at this point will be more credible for that having happened.
The fact is that the Canadian position is to act to reduce sulpher dioxide emissions by making federal money available in concert with provincial and industry money, and we hope that the Government will see through that commitment and negotiate the kinds of agreements which need to be negotiated in the very near future. We will then see an actual empirical reduction in the tonnage of acid rain which is falling here in Canada from Canadian sources.
The Prime Minister said he wanted to go to the bargaining table with clean hands-or at least with cleaner hands because it is an imperfect world-and he did that. He acted on the nitric oxide emissions from automobiles. He went to the bargaining table with a few cards to play. Even though some persons maintain that he threw them all away, I would say he had a few cards to play and it was going to be interesting to see what he came up with, not only on the basis of what action the federal Government had taken itself with respect to acid rain but also in terms of the new relationship with the United States promised by the Prime Minister. What happened? The Canadian position was that action was needed. The American position was that more study was needed. And we came away with a study. To me that means that we accepted the American position.
In my view, Mr. Speaker, and in the view of the New Democratic Party, it would have been far better and more in keeping with the kind of mature relationship, about which the Prime Minister likes to speak when he is speaking about Canada-U.S. relations, for the Prime Minister to have come out of the meeting and told us that they couldn't agree on acid rain, that the President still feels that it is not the kind of problem which demands action, but that we do and we are going to continue to act on a national basis to clean up our sources of acid rain, and that we hope in the long run our continuing action in this respect will finally be persuasive to the Americans. That would have been a much more honest and responsible course of action when talking about Canada-U.S. relations. Instead we have come away with what is obvious to everyone but the Government itself: a cosmetic process designed to save the Prime Minister from having to face up to the fact that he could not get anywhere with the President. Better to have said so. It would not have been such a horrendous failure. It would have been horrendous in the environmental sense but not politically. In my view, that would have been much more acceptable.
The problem is that the Prime Minister has himself in a little bit of a box, given the rhetoric he has been employing on acid rain for the last little while. As is the wont of all political Parties, we tend to blame our political opponents for everything. The Prime Minister has got himself into the position, either through not being totally familiar with the history of the problem or for partisan political reasons, or a combination thereof, of trying to pretend that the deadlock in acid rain negotiations between Canada and the U.S. is completely the fault of the former Liberal Government. With all due respect to the fact that many things can be blamed on the Liberal Party of Canada, the fact is that the blame for acid rain ought to be distributed a bit more evenly.
I refer Members of the House to the last report of the Subcommittee on Acid Rain which was brought back into existence near the end of the last Parliament. It produced a report called Time Lost: A Demand for Action on Acid Rain. This is a unanimous report of an all-Party committee, and I quote from the section on Canada-U.S. relations:
Unfortunately, the political will needed to tackle the problem is lacking in the United States.

-we now felt that the only useful approach to make to our American neighbours would have to be political, inasmuch as the diplomatic initiative had foundered on the intransigence of the Reagan Administration.
In summarizing the events it also points out that there were agreements in place and processes which had begun prior to the election of President Reagan in 1980.
When the Prime Minister said that this expression of concern about acid rain that he obtained in Quebec City from the President was an entirely new thing, well, it is not entirely new from the point of view of successive American administrations. That concern was expressed prior to the election of President Reagan. If anything is new at all, it is that the Prime Minister got those few sentences out of President Reagan. But I maintain that, in view of the fact no real action was agreed to, nothing new has happened and the President felt, out of politeness and in response to the fantastically acquiescent way in which the Prime Minister treated him, that at least he owed the Prime Minister a few utterances with respect to acid rain.
What the Prime Minister has been unable to say, at the Quebec summit or elsewhere, is that there is American culpability here. That has been documented time and time again by members of the various committees set up in this House to study the problem. All we want is a little honest talk about the disagreements which exist between the President and Canadians about acid rain.
March 19, 1985

In speaking about that, I would just like to say a word about what I think friendship with the United States means and what real friendship is all about. I want to begin by saying that the U.S.A. is one of Canada's greatest friends and neighbours. No one is arguing about that. What is at issue is the nature of the friendship. It seems to me that real friends can disagree with each other and still maintain respect for each other. Real friends have a responsibility which sometimes other nations do not have, and it seems to me this is the view of our Party about friendship with the U.S. Sometimes it is only your best friend who can tell you that you acted like a bully at that party the other night or you have been treating someone unkindly, or you really ought to think about the way you are behaving. These are the kinds of things that real friends are for. That is the kind of influence friends can have on each other.
I think this Government misunderstands that nature of friendship and loyalty. As the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) said earlier, loyalty and friendship have a lot to do with being willing to be openly and honestly critical, and that is all we ask of the Prime Minister with respect to acid rain. That is what we ask of him with respect to other areas where Canada should be playing a leading role in being constructively critical of American foreign policy, whether it be in Central America, on the arms race or whatever.
I want to express my own concern about the repeated accusation of anti-Americanism which we hear from the Government benches every time we do not agree with the Government's position concerning Canada-U.S. relations. There are millions and millions of American who do not agree with President Reagan's position on acid rain, or his position on star wars or Central America. Are they anti-American? If we live in a community of democracies where we are free not only to criticize our own Government but the Governments of our neighbours and friends, surely we should be able to speak our mind about what is going on in the United States without being accused of anti-Americanism by this Government. For God's sake, the United States itself abolished the Committee on Un-American Activities; let us not turn the Canadian House of Commons into a committee on un-American activities so that whenever members of the Opposition rise to say they do not agree with the position taken by the Government they are accused of being anti-American. Surely we can have a higher level of debate than that. That is the kind of debate we should be pursuing.
Many of the questions pertaining to Canada-U.S. relations are questions of immense international importance, whether they have to do with the global environment we all share or with the future of the planet itself in terms of the arms race. We ought to be able to have a decent, open and honest debate about these issues without being charged with anti-Americanism.
There are many very serious environmental questions outstanding between Canada and the U.S. The one that comes most quickly to mind is Great Lakes water quality and the fact that seven to eight million Canadians could well be on the verge of having their water supply seriously damaged by the
Supply
leakage of toxins into the Niagara River system from dumps situated on the American side of the border. Action needs to be taken on that front. We need to be firm. We are standing on firm ground on these issues. We do not have anything to apologize for. Surely we ought not to be apologetic for the fact that we are concerned about the drinking water supply of seven to eight million Canadians.
I have been to the U.S. many times and I know a good many Americans, and I think they respect people who stand up for themselves. They respect people who are open, frank and who say just what is going on and what they want people to do. They are not going to be impressed by a lot of back-slapping and head-patting and all the other sorts of things that went on in Quebec City. When it comes to questions of the environment in particular, we are on very firm ground indeed and we should be as frank and honest with the Americans as is necessary in order to get them to see that we are deadly serious about their taking action to reduce acid rain emissions that are crossing our border from their country. We must show them that we are deadly serious about cleaning up the Great Lakes. Of course, we could have better created the impression that we were deadly serious about the quality of Great Lakes water if we had not had the cancellation of the herring gull egg program. Nevertheless, these issues must transcend the day-today mistakes of the Government, and we therefore still have a very strong moral case for speaking to the Americans about that.
I would like to say a final world about the greatest environmental issue of them all. I know that others will be speaking about this. Hopefully, the Hon. Member for New Westmin-ster-Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett) will be able to speak later this afternoon on questions pertaining to security and disarmament. In the final analysis the greatest environmental question of them all is that of nuclear war. It is the prediction of many experts now that any significant nuclear exchange would result in what is called nuclear winter. It would result in environmental damage which would make our concerns about acid rain and toxins in the Great Lakes pale in comparison.
I listened with great interest to the Hon. Member for Saint-Maurice (Mr. Chretien), the former Secretary of State for External Affairs in the Liberal Government. He said that if we create the environment that he believes the present Government is creating by signing these agreements with the Americans with respect to defence, when we get the call saying they want to deploy nuclear weapons on our soil we will not be in a position to say no and that we are kidding ourselves if we think otherwise. Mr. Speaker, we have that environment in Canada.-U.S. relations now. It was created by years and years of Liberal Government. We have been put in a position whereby we are not able to have an independent foreign policy because we are so vulnerable to American action and response, whether economic or otherwise. The Americans play hardball when they want to get their own way with respect to the National Energy Program or whatever it happens to be. They

have a history of being very tough with regard to their own national self-interest.
Over the years we have not developed an economy or a stance with regard to foreign policy which enables us to act independently on short notice. We can thank the actions of successive Liberal Governments for that. The response of the Conservative Government to the environment created by the Liberals is to accept it. They simply say that that is the way the world is and instead of struggling against that reality they accept that environment and do their best within it.
We see this attitude not only with respect to foreign policy but also with respect to foreign investment, and a number of other fronts.
The Conservative policy is not to struggle against the dependence which has been created over the years by successive Liberal administrations, but to accept it as the way the world is and to try to do their very best within it for Canadians. That is a legitimate policy option, but we do not agree with it. We say that in the long term we must struggle against that dominance of our economy and the disability that we have acquired over the years to act independently on the world stage. We invite Canadians to do that by supporting our policy. The Government is quite right in saying that at this point in time it has the mandate. However, we also have a mandate to put forward the alternative view. We must keep reminding Canadians that there is a different way to do things and that we do not have to accept these international realities as if they were the weather which we cannot do anything about.
The world is in part created by human beings. Our social and economic realities are the result of human choices. The world can be changed, but only when and if Canadians join with us and others who are concerned to change the world in that way. That is what we are up to. We are not up to any anti-Americanism or low level carping on a day-to-day political basis. We are trying to make the point that there is an alternative way to exist in the world as Canadians and as a country. We are going to continue to do that, Mr. Speaker.

think he should be quoted, since he is not an expert on the subject. And I am not going to talk about the domination of our economy, because I think our economy is alive and well. Mr. Speaker, on February 5 of this year, using an approach that has now become identified with this Government and that sets us apart from the previous Government of 15 years of confrontation, an approach characterized by conciliation and negociation, thanks to this entirely new style of government, we were able, within just a few months, to achieve with the provinces who are not our enemies but our partners, and we said so quite clearly after the election on September 4, and they believed us and they agreed to work with us, so that with the provinces, we agreed to proceed to a reduction in sulphur emissions, and each province agreed to set quotas to reduce sulphur emissions in Canada.
When the agreement was made public, the Liberal critic for the environment and the NDP critic said, substantially, that there was nothing to it. We thought there was a great deal to it, and our colleagues ... The Hon. Member of the New Democratic Party was obviously supporting the motion presented by the Liberal environmental critic. In any case, I fail to see any clear distinction between the two parties, because they are nearly always saying the same thing, acting as a team and asking questions or supporting each other motions. It was very good timing, Mr. Speaker, because the motion condemning the Government for its failure to take action with respect to the environment came the day before, exactly the day before the public announcement of the Canadian environmental clean-up program, a plan that does not have its equal in any country. So I very much appreciated the timing of my hon. colleague, the Liberal environmental critic. I thought it was most appropriate and almost miraculous, and I said to myself that as long as we have an Opposition that is following the Government's business that closely, we will not have to worry.
That is what we have done. An agreement was signed with seven Canadian provinces, while the Western provinces which are less affected by sulphur emissions offered us their active support, so that this was a Canadian consensus. That enabled us on March 6 to unveil this program under which $300 million are set aside to solve the acid emission problems. It required-a very easy task since we always proceed as a team-the cooperation of twelve federal departments or agencies. On March 6, when we made this
program public, the media were practically unanimous in their praise, saying that no other country had come up with such a program to fight acid rains.

They would go to the United States and insult everybody within hearing distance. They were interviewed on television only to voice further insults, and then they were wondering why joint decisions could not be reached.
Now, these two men are well thought of in both countries. It is recognized, in editorials that they surely will hasten the debate on pollution control.
This is what Mr. Roy has to say: We welcome the appointment of two great artists. Why does he refer to them as artists? Quite simply because scientists have told us all there is to know about acid rain, and there is not much dispute at that level. This is why these two men, experienced as they are in the ramifications and complexity of politics, are asked to debug the issue over the coming year and entrusted with an extremely interesting responsibility. Mr. Davis and Mr. Lewis will be expected to consult on the statutes and regulations pertaining to pollutants.
Canada will be consulted on its own statutes and regulations that govern pollutants, and will be in a position to give its version, its assessment of the regulations. They have been entrusted with the responsibility of enhancing co-operation in research endeavours and here I want to refer to a research report submitted by the Royal Society of Canada to the Environment critic of the Liberal Party when he was Minister of the Environment, in which it was emphasized that research on acid rain was in a terrible mess. This was not said by me, but by the Royal Society of Canada. Clearly, the Environment critic has not said much about that, nor did he try to clear up the mess research on acid rain was in at the federal government level when he was a minister of the Crown and a member of Cabinet.
Therefore, the two appointees will have to discuss at length the question of research, to secure in their respective countries co-ordination of research endeavours and the interrelationship of research activities in both countries. They will also have to look for means to widen the exchange of scientific information in order to avoid duplication, I assume, and make a survey of all of the initiatives taken to improve the Canadian and American environment.
These two men of distinction would not have accepted the responsibility of dealing with that issue simply to sweep it under the carpet. They are men of action. They have accepted the job because they know how important it is for the environment in their respective countries, because they are convinced that they will be able to break the deadlock to which we had come because of the previous government, and to propose concrete initiatives during the upcoming year. They will be facing powerful lobbies, especially from South of the border. They will also be facing powerful unions.
The acid rain problem is tremendously complex, first because it involves huge amounts of money, and secondly

We have continued our efforts begun with the Great Lakes Water Quality agreement of 1972 to protect our joint heritage in the Great Lakes. We want to continue to work co-operatively to understand and control the air and water pollution that respects no borders.
