Mr. Speaker, returning to the first part of the New Democratic Party motion today expressing our concern about possible future linkage between the development of star wars and the uses to which our new Early Warning System may be put and the related matter of the stationing of nuclear weapons on Canadian soil, let me first say a word or two and try to make as clear as I possibly can what our concerns are regarding the moedernization of the DEW Line, now called the North Warning System.
If it were indeed today and for all time a radar system purely used for detection and the communication of information, I do not think any of us would have any great concern. However, when in fact the modernization of the DEW Line is seen by the authorities in the Pentagon as having what they describe as collateral benefits for the development of the President's Strategic Defence Initiative, as star wars is formally called, we are very concerned indeed.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) said this morning that we were sowing fear in the country because of our concern. Quite frankly, The Canadian public is already concerned about the possibility of the escalation of the nuclear arms race and indeed the militarization of outer space. We have not created the concern. The concern has been generated over several years now, and particularly since the President first announced two years ago the possibility of the militarization of space and the extension of the arms race into space. I think it is important to reiterate that. This lies at the root of the concern of the public. It is bad enough having an arms race on land, at sea and in the air, but when it is extended into space, with all the uncontrollable and destabilizing elements that would then be involved, surely the public is quite justified in being concerned.
As I have said, we are not dreaming up the idea that there is a relationship between the modernization of the DEW line and future collateral benefits, to use the words of the Pentagon, for star wars. We have read about these things. In a question to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Nielsen) to which he did not respond, I asked whether or not he had actually read the minutes of the hearings of the committee on armed services of the United States Senate which occurred last spring and again last fall.
It was from reading the minutes of the hearings held before the U.S. Senate committee on armed services that I first realized fully how the Strategic Defence Initiative of the President was to be aided and abetted by certain other developments down the line. I am not saying that this will happen tomorrow. It will happen down the line. After all, star wars is at the research stage now. We have never said that anything would happen tomorrow.
The testimony recorded in those minutes to which I refer explicitly states that both the space shuttle and the modernization of the DEW line would provide collateral benefits to the

Strategic Defence Initiative as it becomes developed and deployed. As Hon. Ministers would discover if they were to read the reports of the Senate committee, there is no question in the minds of the committee members of the United States Senate committee on armed services that the President's Strategic Defence Initiative will go through to deployment. Before I say a few words on that matter, which very much affects the arguments the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of National Defence have been making, let me put on the record the words of Sir Geoffrey Howe regarding the entire star wars concept.
It is clear that this Government has accepted research into star wars and has accepted what the President deems to be the frontier of a ballistic missile defence. I have not heard anyone from the government side, let alone the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), deny their support for the concept of a ballistic missile defence. Indeed, this morning the Minister came quite close to saying that if such a defence is contrary to the ABM treaty, there would have to be negotiations presumably to work our way out of that treaty.
Sir Geoffrey Howe, the Minister of Foreign Affairs for the United Kingdom, has very grave reservations indeed about the development of star wars. As reported in the Ottawa Citizen of March 16, he said the following at a meeting last week:
"the enormous technological expertise and potential of the United States" is very great.
He paid tribute to that technology. I am only reading the parts of the article which are in quotes because I have not yet read the full speech. He then went on to say:
"there would be no advantage in creating a new Maginot Line of the 21st century, liable to be outflanked by relatively simpler and demonstrably cheaper countermeasures."
He went on:
"We must make sure we are not developing what might prove to be only a limited defence against weapons of devastating, destructive force," ...
"We must be especially on our guard against raising hopes that it may be impossible to fulfill."
He then went on to discuss the holes in the dike or the holes in the Maginot Line of the Strategic Defence Initiative of President Reagan. He asks:
"Would these holes in the dike,"... "produce and even encourage a nuclear flood?"
We all feel that we in this House have not had a sufficient discussion of the implications of star wars on the strategic balance and indeed we have not had sufficient discussion of its technical feasibility let alone its strategic desirability. I gather from the BBC news that Sir Geoffrey Howe's remarks are the top story in the United Kingdom today joined with the story of very similar remarks made yesterday by the West German Foreign Minister, Hans Dietrich Genscher, who was again questioning both the technical feasibility and the strategic desirability of star wars.
Again our Ministers will say to us that they have only approved the Reagan initiative so far as research is concerned. The Minister from the United Kingdom and West Germany are questioning the research. That is the point I wish to get through to our Ministers. We and the NDP are not the only ones questioning the research. Foreign Ministers of the United Kingdom and West Germany are questioning it because they do see it as being destabilizing. They do see it as changing the entire strategic balance. They do see it as being an escalation of the arms race into space.

The question has been raised whether or not more questions should be asked. I am in the hands of the committee on that question and will look forward to hearing from the chairman.

I have two points: first, that is not what we are asking. What we are asking, which is quite different, is a commitment from the Government now

The speech dealt with star wars, and what we and the Canadian people are concerned about is the star wars equipment on both sides, not just that of the United States. We want both sides to abandon their star wars equipment, not just the United States. The reason the U.S. has to develop the star wars equipment is to keep up with the U.S.S.R. We hope that at the top they will both agree to disband everything and get rid of all nuclear weapons as well as chemical weapons.
Russia has a number of types of star wars equipment. They have RORSAT, a radar ocean-reconnaissance satellite. This is an advanced piece of weaponry. It can probably detect destroyer and aircraft carrier-size ships in good weather. The Russians also have ERORSAT, which is another electronic intelligence ocean-reconnaissance satellite and which is used with RORSAT for detecting and tracking of naval vessels in open or coastal waters. If we are to sit back and do nothing and allow them to develop this kind of equipment, we will have nothing with which to protect ourselves. We would be absolutely vulnerable. The ERORSAT is the Soviet-based space system which is possibly most capable of sea target detection, so you can see they are way ahead of us. They also have ELINT III. This is the third generation electronic intelligence satellite. They operate in a record playback mode and can locate pulsed emitters to a best accuracy of about 10 kilometres. They can detect radars on operating air fields if they use pulsed emitters and possibly provide an after-the-fact assessment of the location of airborne warning and control systems. The Russians also have the advanced ELINT, and experts anticipate deployment of that system by the end of 1985.
I do not understand the NDP and its position that it is just the United States that we have to concern ourselves about. We have to concern ourselves about the Warsaw Pact countries with nuclear and chemical weapons, as well as star wars equipment, and we have to be sure we can defend ourselves against their advanced development. So we in the Conservative Party want to see disarmament on both sides, not unilateral
disarmament. Criticism should be levelled also at the Warsaw Pact countries. They are the ones who are ahead of us. I have never spoken to any Canadian who wants just us on this side to disarm. We know that that would be absolute suicide. That would be the end of us for all time.
There is no such a thing as not having to co-operate with the United States. The majority of Canadians now understand why we have to test the Cruise missile and they understand why we have to do research into star wars. It is because of the Warsaw Pact build-up. So it is a two way street. If we did not have to develop star wars we would have all the money in the world to wipe out acid rain. We want to wish the negotiators the best of luck on this question, but we want both sides to disarm.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs is going to Russia in a couple of weeks and I am sure he will be discussing our concerns with the Russians. We want them to eliminate their star wars equipment and chemical warfare weapons and all the rest. We want disarmament on both sides, not just this side.

Mr. Speaker, I want to address the North Warning System element of this debate. I want to do it in the political context in which the discussion is taking place this afternoon. Contrary to the belief of the Hon. Member who has just resumed her seat, I will be appearing before the Standing Committee on Thursday at or about 3.30 in the afternoon. I sincerely hope that she will not be ill at that time so that she will be able to be present and put forth whatever questions she did not have the opportunity to put forth because of her absence when the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) appeared before that committee.
I would like to open my remarks today, Mr. Speaker, with the following quote:
Canada is a veteran of the two world wars and of Korea. We have acquired our national sovereignty honourably, in important measure through the enormous sacrifice of generations of Canadians who with genuine courage-and in many cases, with their very lives-spoke for our unshakeable commitment to freedom, our unquenchable belief in democracy. Having thus acquired our independence, we shall surrender no part of it any time in any circumstance.
That was the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) speaking at Quebec City over the weekend. That is the stance of the Government with respect to the several questions which members of the Opposition, and others outside of this place, have been raising in order to sow fear and doubt in the minds of Canadians with respect to the real purpose of NWS.
The Member who just resumed her seat said herself that she would not be alarmed, as most Canadians would not be alarmed, if the purpose of NWS was radar surveillance. I see her nodding in affirmation from where she is standing behind the curtains. However, she will not accept that NWS is exactly that. In upgrading and modernizing NWS we are precisely replacing the system that is in place. The assistance which that system gives to civil aviation is a dimension which has not been addressed. If the Hon. Member had flown as many hours as I have in the north using that system, she would have a different view. That is all that NWS is intended to do and will do.
What the Leader of the NDP (Mr. Broadbent) has called the most radical change in Canada-U.S. relations in this century, in reference to the Quebec summit, is simply a return to the civility and readiness to live up to responsibilities that are implicit in treaties that this country has been a party to for many years. As co-signers of NORAD we undertook certain defence obligations embracing the defence of this continent and of the free world. We are living up to those commitments. The only radical change is that our Government is acting as though we intended to live up to those arrangements and to be active and participating partners in our own defence.
I need only refer you to history, Sir, to indicate the very short shrift of those nations which have left the responsibility of their defence to others. That is precisely what the NDP is advocating. If we have learned one thing from history, it is that countries which lose interest in their defence come to lose their liberty, freedom and independence. That is what they are advocating over there. They are advocating the hands-off approach. They believe that we can put off the fact that we are now living in a nuclear age. The NDP appears to believe that

It has always been the policy of his Party, no matter how much the Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill hastens to scurry away from that position at this late date.
I can only describe the position of the Leader of the Official Opposition as an enigma wrapped in obscurity. He approves our objectives. He whole-heartedly supports closer relations. He wants to live up to our responsibilities. He is just put out because we were the ones to do these things. He and his Party had 10 years in which to do them but they did little or nothing. When the Liberal Party left office, relations with the United States were at their lowest ebb since 1812. His attitude of trying to ride in both directions at the same time is certainly not conducive to creative relations. What is really eating their hearts out, Mr. Speaker, is that the summit in Quebec was a success, that there was real progress made. That is what is eating them.
As an aside, I would indicate that the summit has done more than any other single event in my recollection to sow the seeds of national unity in this country. He again trotted out the Trudeau dictum of even-handed justice to both superpowers. This demonstrates once again the Liberal party's inability to draw the line between our friends and those who have not demonstrated the kind of friendship and understanding of western democracy that we expect from friends. In the very next breath, he said, "Of course the Americans are our friends". We agree with that. However, where we seem to part
company is that we intend to give our friends the benefit of the doubt.
As I have already mentioned, there is some excuse for the NDP, given its traditional distrust of the Americans, but there is no excuse for the carping, critical, uninformed and petty attitude of members of the Official Opposition. I would ask them, in all sincerity, to look around the world and gain a perception of present realities and future opportunities.
Canadians are entitled to a real and honest appreciation of the real problems of our time. What we got from the Leader of the Official Opposition was warmed over Trudeauism. Tom Axworthy may be gone but his spirit lived on this morning in the sorry, sad diatribe of the Leader of the Official Opposition.
The Prime Minister of Canada and President Reagan confirmed in Quebec honest and positive policies and progress between our two countries. They confirmed that friends and allies must work together. They confirmed that friends and allies must be honest with each other. They confirmed that friends and allies must make real efforts to keep lines of communication open. That was a historic restoration of a relationship which has been allowed to wither and die under 16 years of Liberal office.
At Quebec, the Prime Minister addressed himself to the realities of which Canadians are all aware each day of our lives and took steps to restore a relationship of civility and honest endeavour between Canada and the United States.
The benefits of that epochal action will flow into every phase of our economic and commercial life in this country in the months ahead. No amount of carping and criticism from the NDP and no amount of nostalgic posturing-for it can only be called that-by the Leader of the Opposition will alter the fact that a powerful blow for Canadian sovereignty was struck at Quebec over the weekend. Our Government has taken a step forward in history while the Grits are dragging their feet and the NDP is at least dragging its prejudices, if not something worse.

Mr. Speaker, there is quite a contrast between the glowing terms with which the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) describes the Quebec meeting last weekend and the comments by a conservatively inclined newspaper of Toronto, The Toronto Sun. The column written by Claire Hoy, from which I will quote briefly, just to put things back into a different perspective at least, reads:
Like a small child tugging at his mother's skirts for attention. Prime Minister Brian Mulroney yesterday took our natural intercontinental friendship with the U.S. into the uncomfortable realm of mindless obedience to a powerful parent.
The so-called Shamrock summit-is supposed to demonstrate how two relatively equal sovereign states can resolve their common differences.
Instead, it has all the appearance of an American master being greeted by a panting Canadian lapdog, wagging his tail furiously hoping to have a few bones tossed in his direction.
The first and most important bone was an agreement by the two leaders to name former Ontario Premier Bill Davis and former U.S. Transportation Secretary Andrew Lewis as special envoys to resolve the joint issue of acid rain.
The appointment is instructive because it demonstrates how stage-managed this event is, and underscores the fact that if you want to defuse the volatile political issue, nobody could bury it better than Davis.
This, of course, is by way of background commentary. I would not want to elaborate further in that direction. What I would like to do briefly is to bring to your attention the fact, as a result of the announcement on acid rain over the weekend, for the first time this Progressive Conservative Government is facing an environmental community of non-governmental groups which, for the first time since election, are not supportive of the Conservative Government decision on acid rain.
Why is that coming about for the first time? Evidently there is profound disappointment and not only just within the ranks of non-governmental groups.
President Reagan, if you look at the record, said in Quebec City just about the same on acid rain as he did in 1981 when he came to Ottawa. Can that be called progress? I suppose in Progressive Conservative terms that can be called progress, but the Conservatives will be alone with that kind of assessment.
In Quebec City the Prime Minister and President Reagan failed to give leadership on this important question. They side-stepped the issue and really the winner on that day was the National Coal Association. The Executive Vice-President, Danny Ellerman, speaking on acid rain said, "Acid rain is a subterfuge". This is the same Coal Association whose President, Carl Bagge, wrote to the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) some weeks ago complimenting him on his stand on acid rain. Isn't that a strange source for praise, Mr. Speaker?
The question is, why did the Prime Minister fail to give leadership? Why did he give away Canada's bargaining position two months ago? Why did he not draw to the attention of the President that smoke-stack emissions in Canada are 4.6 million tonnes compared with 26 million tonnes in the United States, theirs being over five times ours and we being downwind of theirs? Why did he not bring to their attention that in terms of research in Canada we spend on a per capita basis twice as much as the U.S.? Why did he not bring to their attention that in terms of car emissions, tonnage per year, U.S. emissions are ten times ours? Did he make any use of the memorandum of understanding which was signed in August 1980? Why did he feel he had to go to Quebec City on his environmental knees instead of putting the issue squarely to President Reagan for solution because it can only be dealt with at the political level?
Scientific communities in Canada and in the United States have agreed that there is enough scientific knowledge to move with a decision. This statement was made back in 1983 by the United States National Academy of Sciences. In essence, the Prime Minister agreed to further research.
It is quite clear from the interventions this afternoon that the Progressive Conservative Government is desperately trying
March 19, 1985

to rewrite history and to convince the Canadian public that the acid rain story began on September 4, 1984. It might be worthwhile to put on the record the fact that on August 5, 1980 the memorandum of intent on acid rain between Canada and the United States was signed. It raised a lot of hope, and quite rightly so. We thought we could continue in the fine tradition of settling trans-boundary environmental issues jointly, as we did with Lake Erie and on many other occasions. Efforts followed, but when it became evident that not even William Ruckelshaus, in charge of the Environmental Protection Agency in Washington, could convince his own Government to proceed with a control program in the winter of 1983-84, we had to make a decision on our own. On March 6, 1984, provincial and federal Ministers of the Environment jointly decided to go for a cut of 50 per cent by 1984. On March 20 of the same year, here in Ottawa, nine friendly and similarly inclined nations joined us in a declaration whereby we would commit ourselves to a minimum cut of 30 per cent by 1993. In May of that year, the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, through its Minister, produced a paper for the modernization of non-ferrous smelters, indicating how a reduction in emissions could be achieved. In June of that year, the political commitment was renewed again in Ottawa. Also we had the satisfaction in Munich of seeing the number go up from 10 to 20 nations committed to join in the 30 per cent cut by 1993.
The focus is now shifting away from Ottawa and Washington. Apparently it is in the hands of Messrs. Davis and Lewis. We should ask ourselves what will bring Americans to the negotiating table to cut down S02 emissions. There are only two considerations which one has to keep in mind. Either the U.S. Government will be motivated by domestic economic considerations-and evidently those considerations have not yet emerged in their political mind-or by international pressures by the international community urging the United States administration to join this minimum group of nations willing to cut down the emissions by 30 per cent by 1993.
We have an opportunity between now and next July in Helsinki when EEC member nations will be meeting to sign the protocol. I urge the Government to pay attention to this opportunity. It is through that group that we might be able to bring the United States Government to the table to join with us in the cuts.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- CANADA-UNITED STATES RELATIONS
speechtext: I declare the amendment to the motion lost.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- CANADA-UNITED STATES RELATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, unless there is some reason for Members to change their mind, I think the same vote could be recorded on the main motion.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- CANADA-UNITED STATES RELATIONS
speechtext: I sense a disposition on this matter.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Minister of State (Government House Leader); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- CANADA-UNITED STATES RELATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as much as I enjoy votes these days, I will agree with the proposition being put forward. I love those votes!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- CANADA-UNITED STATES RELATIONS
speechtext: The Hon. Member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid) on a point of order.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- CANADA-UNITED STATES RELATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was not here for the first vote, but 1 wish to be counted for the second vote.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- CANADA-UNITED STATES RELATIONS
speechtext: The question is, Mr. Speaker, which way does he want to be counted?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- CANADA-UNITED STATES RELATIONS
speechtext: I think the Member indicated he wanted to be counted the same way as the gentleman beside him was counted.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- CANADA-UNITED STATES RELATIONS
speechtext: We can't assume that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- CANADA-UNITED STATES RELATIONS
speechtext:
I declare the motion lost.
It being 6.16 p.m., this House stands adjourned until tomorrow at two o'clock, pursuant to Standing Order 2(1).
The House adjourned at 6.16 p.m.
Wednesday, March 20, 1985
